Endocrinology · published research

Hypothyroidism

Summary of the Evidence

Berisha-Muharremi and Humolli 2026 reviewed six human studies published from 2010 through 2025 and presented a narrative synthesis without pooled estimates. Reports describe favorable patient-reported or biochemical outcomes in some settings, but the designs, co-interventions, and outcomes differ. Four Höfling publications follow the same 43-person randomized cohort, so publication counts exceed the number of independent trials. Whether the 2023 and 2025 Berisha-Muharremi reports include overlapping participants is unclear.

Human and clinical evidence

A 15-person single-arm pilot reported lower levothyroxine requirements and anti-TPO levels after treatment, while anti-thyroglobulin antibodies did not significantly change. Without a control group, the observed changes cannot be separated from medication management or other changes (Höfling et al. 2010).

A later sham-controlled trial reported lower anti-TPO levels and improved thyroid-ultrasound echogenicity in the active group, but no anti-thyroglobulin difference. Four related Höfling publications report Doppler, antibody, growth-factor, and long-term outcomes from this same cohort. The long-term report found that levothyroxine requirements remained lower in the active group, while antibody levels no longer differed between groups (Höfling et al. 2012; Höfling et al. 2013; Höfling et al. 2014; Höfling et al. 2018).

A nonrandomized comparison of 350 people reported more favorable thyroid-hormone, anti-TPO, and levothyroxine outcomes when PBM was added to vitamin D, iron, and selenium supplementation. The co-interventions and nonrandom allocation prevent a clear estimate of the contribution from PBM (Ercetin et al. 2020).

A 2023 feasibility comparison enrolled 74 women, but only 38 completed follow-up. Thyroid-hormone and antibody measures improved in the PBM-plus-supplement group, although baseline differences and substantial attrition limit interpretation. A 2025 comparative study from the same research group reported favorable TSH, anti-TPO, and thyroid-volume outcomes over 12 months. A smaller proportion of the PBM-plus-supplement group had free T4 within the reference range than the supplement-only group at follow-up. Both studies combined PBM with supplements and lifestyle advice, and participant overlap between the reports is unclear (Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2023; Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2025).

A 46-person sham-controlled trial reported better quality of life and oxidative-stress measures, but no between-group difference in thyroid hormones or autoimmunity at three months (Tunç et al. 2024). A separate 2026 sham-controlled trial reported greater improvement in fatigue and behavioral symptom scores at three months. It adds patient-reported evidence but does not establish restored thyroid function (Tunç et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

A propylthiouracil-induced hypothyroidism mouse experiment found no measurable improvement in thyroid function after red-light treatment (Mun et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Clinical protocols applied near-infrared light transcutaneously over the thyroid, but dose and schedule varied. The 2010 pilot used 830-nm laser light at 50 mW with reported fluences of 38–108 J/cm². The related Höfling randomized cohort used 830 nm at 50 mW, a reported fluence of 707 J/cm², 40 seconds per point, and ten sessions twice weekly for five weeks (Höfling et al. 2010; Höfling et al. 2013).

Ercetin et al. used 850 nm at 28.57 J/cm² per point for six sessions over three days. The Berisha-Muharremi comparisons used 820 nm at 32 J/cm² per point, 20 seconds at eight points, and six sessions over three weeks. The 2024 and 2026 sham-controlled trials used 850 nm, 100 mW, 28.57 J/cm² per point, 20 seconds at eight points, and six sessions over three weeks. Supplements, lifestyle advice, and thyroid-medication management were part of some protocols (Ercetin et al. 2020; Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2023; Tunç et al. 2024; Tunç et al. 2026). These studies do not establish an optimal wavelength, dose, or schedule.

Interpretation

The most direct positive findings concern short-term fatigue or quality of life and levothyroxine requirements in one randomized cohort. Controlled findings for thyroid hormones and antibodies are mixed, and favorable results from supplement-comparison studies cannot be attributed to PBM alone. A lower replacement requirement in a study does not establish remission or justify stopping prescribed thyroid medication.

Publications and records

13 publications

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Levothyroxine requirement, Höfling et al. 2013 randomized trial. At nine months, the mean dose was 38.59 ± 20.22 µg/day with PBM (n=23) and 106.88 ± 22.90 µg/day with sham (n=20), p<0.001. Levothyroxine was withdrawn after treatment and restarted as needed (Höfling et al. 2013).

Levothyroxine and anti-TPO, Höfling et al. 2010 single-arm pilot. Mean levothyroxine dose fell from 96 ± 22 to 38 ± 23 µg/day by nine months, and 7 of 15 participants stopped replacement. Mean anti-TPO fell from 982 ± 530 to 579 ± 454 U/mL (p=0.016). This is an uncontrolled within-group change. Anti-thyroglobulin did not significantly decrease (Höfling et al. 2010).

TSH and anti-TPO, Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2023 feasibility comparison. Thirty-eight of 74 participants completed follow-up. Baseline-to-six-month median TSH was 3.50 (1.94–4.65) to 1.25 (0.46–1.51) mIU/L with PBM plus supplements and 2.92 (1.38–3.80) to 3.05 (2.50–4.05) mIU/L with supplements alone. Median anti-TPO was 523.60 (291.75–652.55) to 88.25 (62.25–129.50) IU/mL and 219.75 (70.45–538.97) to 171.85 (87.12–443.60) IU/mL, respectively. These are observed group medians, not a randomized treatment-effect estimate (Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2023).

TSH, anti-TPO, and thyroid volume, Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2025 comparison. Ninety-seven of 98 participants completed follow-up. At baseline and 12 months, mean TSH was 3.19 ± 2.19 to 1.40 ± 0.36 mIU/L with PBM plus supplements and 3.43 ± 3.18 to 2.52 ± 0.74 mIU/L with supplements alone (time-by-group p=0.001, partial η²=0.066). Median anti-TPO was 353 (123–552) to 88 (60–123) IU/mL versus 266.75 (102.02–560.47) to 174.5 (99.97–450) IU/mL (p<0.0001, partial η²=0.177). Mean thyroid volume was 16.93 ± 3.24 to 14.28 ± 4.23 mL versus 14.88 ± 3.24 to 15.04 ± 3.69 mL (p<0.0001, partial η²=0.127). At follow-up, free T4 was within the reference range for 47% of the PBM-plus-supplement group and 85% of the comparison group (Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2025).

Fatigue, Tunç et al. 2026 sham-controlled trial. At three months, Fatigue Impact Scale scores changed from 69.83 ± 35.49 to 30.00 ± 22.28 with PBM and from 63.80 ± 22.12 to 58.80 ± 20.14 with sham (between-group t=6.386, p<0.001). Fatigue Severity Scale scores changed from 42.50 ± 14.35 to 29.40 ± 13.82 and from 40.43 ± 12.17 to 37.57 ± 11.44, respectively (between-group t=3.852, p=0.001) (Tunç et al. 2026).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Fatigue and symptoms: low-to-moderate certainty for short-term improvement. One sham-controlled trial found improvement at three months (Tunç et al. 2026).

Quality of life: low certainty for short-term improvement. A small sham-controlled trial reported benefit, with no short-term thyroid-hormone or antibody difference (Tunç et al. 2024).

Reduced levothyroxine requirement: low certainty. Findings are supported mainly by one small randomized cohort and nonrandomized supplement-comparison studies (Höfling et al. 2013; Berisha-Muharremi et al. 2023).

Restored thyroid function or disease remission: very low certainty. Controlled biochemical findings are mixed, and the reviewed studies do not establish remission (Tunç et al. 2024; Berisha-Muharremi and Humolli 2026).

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Fatigue and quality-of-life results come from two small sham-controlled trials with short follow-up and limited independent replication. Levothyroxine findings come from one 43-person randomized cohort reported in several papers, plus nonrandomized supplement-comparison studies. Medication changes, concurrent supplements, attrition, and unresolved participant overlap limit confidence that PBM alone accounts for biochemical changes. These limits differ by outcome, so the ratings remain separate (Höfling et al. 2013; Tunç et al. 2024; Tunç et al. 2026).
